title: Causal Inference Framework for Multi-Modal Data Fusion
abstract: This paper introduces a novel causal inference framework designed specifically for multi-modal data fusion. The core challenge in leveraging diverse data sources – encompassing images, text, and sensor readings – lies in understanding the underlying causal relationships between them. Traditional data analysis methods often struggle with this complexity, leading to inaccurate predictions and flawed decision-making. Our framework addresses this gap by integrating causal graph modeling, structure learning algorithms, and Bayesian networks to construct a multi-modal causal graph. This graph then serves as a foundation for inference and reasoning across the different data modalities. The system aims to identify direct and indirect causal links, allowing for more robust predictions and interventions. This work provides a theoretical foundation and a methodological approach for tackling the critical issue of causal discovery within multi-modal data scenarios. The proposed framework offers a significant advancement in the field of data fusion and causal inference, paving the way for more reliable and interpretable AI systems.

title: Brandt's Bat: A Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by Echolocation
abstract: This paper presents Brandt's Bat, a novel metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the echolocation behavior of bats. The algorithm leverages the principles of bat sonar, utilizing a population of bats and a dynamic landscape to explore and optimize solutions. The core of Brandt's Bat lies in its "frequency-modulated" and "phase-modulated" parameters, which govern bat movement and decision-making. These parameters are dynamically adjusted based on the fitness of the solutions in the population. The algorithm employs a circular search space and a stochastic update mechanism to navigate the solution space effectively. The performance of Brandt's Bat is evaluated on several benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions within reasonable computational time. The algorithm's parameters are carefully tuned to balance exploration and exploitation, leading to robust performance across a range of problem types. The key innovations of Brandt's Bat include the dynamic adjustment of modulation frequencies and phases, and the utilization of a circular search space to mimic the bat's continuous monitoring of its environment. The results indicate that Brandt's Bat presents a promising alternative to established metaheuristic algorithms, particularly in scenarios where rapid exploration and adaptation are crucial.

title: The use of Guided Generation to Enhance Extraction of Information from Technical Research Papers
authors: Sandia National Laboratories (SNL-NM), Albuquerque, NM (United States)
abstract: This project studied whether "guided generation"-forcing a Large Language Model (LLM) to answer a question using a structured format-helps extract information from technical research literature better than letting it answer free form.Finding answers in technical literature has historically meant keyword search plus manual review; LLMs are changing that, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which grounds an LLM's answers in retrieved source passages, is an alternative that is explored in the AI community 1 .Using a corpus built from the International Symposium for Testing and Failure Analysis (ISTFA) proceedings 2 , we generated answers under ten conditions-a no-retrieval baseline, two synthetic degraded conditions for validating the judge, five RAG retrieval conditions, the guided generation condition, and "pondering," a two-turn condition.We tested these with two completion models (Mistral-Small 24B and GPT-OSS 120B) and two embedding backends (a local Model2Vec embedder and Google's EmbeddingGemma).All answers (~431 per configuration) were scored 0-10 by a fixed LLM-as-judge, which we first validated: it ranks deliberately degraded answers monotonically (No-RAG baseline > Mostly Right > False), confirming it scores correctness rather than fluency.Retrieval reliably improved quality over the no-RAG baseline, with most gains within two to three documents.Critically, guided generation did not materially help and actively harmed the smaller model (-1.9 to -2.3 points versus plain RAG), while remaining neutral on the larger model; a gentler prompting variant was neutral throughout.The cheaper local embedder matched EmbeddingGemma on median quality from two documents onward.Across the two models and two embedders tested, the evidence argues for simple, shallow RAG with a capable model rather than elaborate guided generation or multi-turn response-especially for small, locally deployed models.

title: Site adaptation of global solar irradiance (GHI) at Cota Cota, Peru
abstract: Abstract In this work a Site Adaptation process was performed on the global horizontal solar irradiance (GHI) estimates of the MDSSFTD (Meteosat Downward Surface Shortwave Total and Diffuse Shortwave Fluxes) product of the LSA-SAF satellite database, using an artificial neural network of the multilayer perceptron (MLP) type. The adapted values are compared against hourly measurements obtained at the Cota Cota station (Caylloma, Arequipa) through the rRMSE and rMBE metrics. As a result, the MLP model corrects the initial bias of the LSA-SAF model and significantly reduces the error dispersion in the training and test stages by approximately 6% and 7%, respectively. With this information, the data availability could be temporarily extended.

title: Assessing artificial marketing intelligence
abstract: Foundational marketing knowledge, from theories of consumer behavior to segmentation frameworks and pricing models, supports effective marketing decisions, yet managers often struggle to access and apply it in practice. This paper evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can function as scalable knowledge systems that make foundational marketing knowledge broadly accessible. Specifically, we assess what LLMs “know” about marketing and how effectively they can reason with and apply that knowledge. We construct a comprehensive dataset of over 30,000 questions drawn from instructor materials of 25 widely used marketing textbooks and assess LLM performance across three dimensions: domain knowledge, reasoning capabilities, and user interaction. Across models and providers, current LLMs achieve high accuracy (84%–94%), demonstrate near-complete coverage of marketing topics, and show strong performance on recall and understanding. Performance declines on higher-order reasoning tasks, though newer reasoning models close these gaps substantially. Experimental manipulations of these questions suggest that AI performance reflects more than simple memorization. In a human benchmarking study, LLMs substantially outperform all sampled human respondent groups, while showing complementary strengths relative to more advanced human reasoning. These findings indicate that LLMs have crossed an important capability threshold: they now provide reliable, on-demand access to much of the discipline’s foundational knowledge, with important implications for how marketing knowledge is disseminated, taught, and applied.

title: Systems for Context Data
abstract: This chapter explores the components and methodologies of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline, emphasizing freshness mechanisms and context data infrastructure. It introduces the CRAFT dimensions—complete, retrievable, accurate, fresh, traceable—as a framework for evaluating data readiness. The chapter examines vector databases, coverage management, embedding, indexing, and transformation pipelines, alongside knowledge domain taxonomy, coverage tracking, gap identification, and prioritization. Enterprise AI infrastructure spending reached $1.5 billion in 2025 for storage, retrieval, and orchestration. Case studies of Georgia-Pacific, AWS, and Klarna illustrate knowledge capture, data operations, and AI assistant scope limitations. Document ingestion infrastructure, including connectors, parsers, and loaders, is examined. The chapter highlights chunking, recommending recursive splitting at 400–512 tokens with 10–20% overlap, and notes that late chunking improves retrieval by up to 6.5 percentage points. Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), embedding fine-tuning, and vector database categories are discussed, including pgvector. Hybrid search using BM25, vector similarity, and Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is covered. Privacy risks, PII detection, RBAC, RAGAS evaluation, Change Data Capture (CDC), and blue-green deployment are also addressed. The chapter concludes with hallucination reduction in medical and legal settings and the importance of traceability, source verification, freshness monitoring, and maintaining system integrity across production RAG pipelines.

title: Modelstamp: Pre-Deserialization Verification of Machine-Learning Artifacts and Runtime Environment State
abstract: Persisted machine-learning models can remain byte-identical while the software environments in which they are loaded evolve, creating a verification problem that artifact integrity checks alone cannot expose. This paper presents Modelstamp, a lightweight Python persistence library for verifying artifact integrity and represented runtime-environment state before deserialization. At persistence time, Modelstamp associates a serialized artifact with a sidecar JSON manifest containing a SHA-256 digest, runtime metadata, and installed versions from a bounded tracked-package set; a separately recorded model-relevant subset determines which package versions participate in drift comparison. Optional HMAC authentication supports workflows in which the producer and verifier share a secret key. At verification time, the artifact and represented current environment are checked against this recorded evidence before the model is deserialized. Modelstamp is evaluated using 14 controlled environment-drift scenarios, eight controlled trust-boundary scenarios, and an artifact-size scaling benchmark from 10 MiB to 1 GiB. The controlled drift experiments behaved as specified across relevant dependency changes, unchanged environments, and unrelated environmental changes, including broader noise controls. The trust-boundary experiments similarly confirmed both intended detections and expected limitations, including shared-key forgery and replay. Median verification time increased from 0.032 s at 10 MiB to 3.334 s at 1 GiB, with measured throughput of approximately 307-312 MiB/s in the benchmark environment. These results characterize Modelstamp as a complementary pre-deserialization reference-state verification control rather than as a replacement for dependency-management systems, malicious-model detection, safe deserialization, or public publisher authentication.

title: Griotte: Verified Compartmentalisation via Capabilities
abstract: CHERIoT is a novel hardware-software co-design that leverages hardware capabilities to define a notion of compartment, in a minimalistic capability-based OS, CHERIoT RTOS. By default, compartments are isolated to limit damage in case of bugs or malicious behaviour. To allow cross-compartment communication, the OS provides a privileged component, called the switcher. The switcher provides an interface for cross-compartment calls, while enforcing isolation between compartments and guaranteeing stack safety. Together with hardware capabilities, the switcher is critical to enforce the security guarantees of the CHERIoT compartment model. The design of CHERIoT raises two questions: First, how can one formalise the informal notion of compartmentalisation that CHERIoT compartments are designed to provide? And second, given that the safety properties of CHERIoT hinge on the complementary roles of the capability machine and of the switcher, does the design of CHERIoT enforce the desired security properties? In this paper, we introduce Griotte and Griotte OS, idealised but faithful versions of the CHERIoT machine and the CHERIoT RTOS, which we use to answer these two questions: First, we formally capture the aforementioned security guarantees in the form of a continuation-based logical relation which captures the combined behaviour of the switcher and of the capability machine. And second, we define a specification for the Griotte switcher that enforces those guarantees, and prove that the implementation meets the specification. We demonstrate Griotte on a range of key scenarios illustrating different aspects of CHERIoT, including integrity of the local state in the presence of memory sharing with unknown code. Our approach is modular: we verify compartments individually, and then compose their specifications. Together, our contributions give a solid formal foundation to the design of CHERIoT.

title: User Representation via Cross Multi-source Behavior Pre-training for Mobile Games
abstract: User representation pre-training has become a fundamental paradigm for alleviating data sparsity in downstream personalization tasks. However, existing studies predominantly focus on single-app or app-level behaviors, overlooking the inherently cross-source and multi-granular nature of user activities on mobile devices. At the device level, user intent emerges from complex interactions among heterogeneous behavior sources and hierarchical action structures, posing challenges that cannot be addressed by conventional app-centric modeling. To tackle this issue, we propose CM-PTM, a novel Cross Multi-source Behavior Pre-Training Model tailored for mobile game user representation learning on device-level behavioral logs. CM-PTM employs hierarchical cascaded mask-then-predict proxy tasks that first infer the source of the next behavior and then progressively refine predictions at the app-action level. This design enables unified modeling of cross-source dependencies and fine-grained behavioral dynamics within a single pre-training paradigm. Extensive experiments on large-scale real-world mobile datasets demonstrate that CM-PTM effectively captures users' endogenous interests and consistently delivers significant performance gains on downstream mobile game recommendation tasks.

title: Can Scene Text Recognition Read Rare Compositions?
abstract: Scene text recognition is reported as 89--97% accurate on the six standard benchmarks, and the problem is widely treated as saturated. We present an alternative reading. When the same test images are stratified jointly by ground-truth word rarity and character n-gram novelty against a reference corpus, accuracy at the rare-word x rare-trigram corner of the resulting 5x5 grid drops 10--18 pt below the q3/q3 centre across nine English specialised recognisers, and the same direction (corner below centre) holds on all 13 of 13 (language, model) pairs we test across four writing systems (Latin, Han, Han+kana, Arabic). The drop is not a capacity bottleneck. A 6x vision-backbone scale-up (CLIP4STR-Base 158M -> CLIP4STR-Huge 1.0B, OpenCLIP ViT-H/14 LAION-2B) leads every benchmark in aggregate accuracy yet leaves the stress corner unchanged (86.9 -> 86.5, within paired-bootstrap noise). Four converging probes--layer-wise probing, confidence-when-wrong, attention re-balancing, and a cross-script commit-vs-abstain error split--localise the failure to the autoregressive decoder's lexical prior. We then ask how much of the gap existing techniques recover. Of 16 non-architectural mitigations, the largest mean q5/q5 gain is +1.3 pt and none clears the paired-bootstrap noise floor; the only intervention that does is the architectural shift from autoregressive to CTC decoding (SVTRv2, +2.5 pt, p=0.02, n=474). A confidence-routed AR-CTC ensemble adds a directionally consistent +0.6 pt that stays within noise, and its dominant learned coefficient is each model's own minimum-softmax confidence--independently echoing the mechanism above. No configuration we test improves both the compositional corner and aggregate accuracy. The rare-input long tail thus points to architectural change rather than added capacity.

title: UAV-borne Magnetic and Radiometric Data: Advancing Processing, Fusion, Machine Learning, and Inversion
abstract: Uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) magnetic and gamma-ray spectrometric surveys can collect geophysical data at higher spatial density than conventional airborne systems. This makes them useful for geological mapping and mineral exploration at local scales. However, added detail does not automatically lead to better geological interpretation. UAV measurements are affected by detector footprint, terrain, flight geometry, sampling, counting uncertainty, and spatial dependence. This thesis examines how these factors control the geological information recovered from UAV magnetic and radiometric surveys. The first part investigates UAV-borne gamma-ray spectrometry. It evaluates how terrain, detector height, and platform motion influence radiometric measurements. It also develops a terrain-correction approach that accounts for source-detector geometry and terrain visibility. The results show that acquisition effects can produce spatial patterns that resemble geological variation if they are not considered during processing and interpretation. The thesis then introduces RadSIMU, a survey-scale simulation framework for UAV-borne gamma-ray spectrometry. The simulator tests how flight speed, line spacing, integration time, terrain, and detector footprint affect spatial feature recovery. The results show that recoverable detail is mainly controlled by detector footprint and sampling density. Longer integration times reduce counting noise, but they do not recover information lost through footprint averaging or undersampling. Building on this physical understanding, a terrain-aware inversion method is developed to estimate near-surface radioelement distributions from UAV gamma-ray data. The inversion links airborne measurements to surface radioelement concentrations through a forward model that includes detector footprint, attenuation, terrain visibility, acquisition geometry, and measurement uncertainty. The recovered models improve spatial interpretation and show the resolution limits imposed by measurement physics. also evaluates supervised machine learning for lithological mapping using UAV magnetic and radiometric predictors. It shows that random validation can overestimate performance when spatial dependence is present. Spatial validation gives a more realistic assessment of predictive skill. Finally, radiometric evidence is used to evaluate geological constraints applied in magnetic inversion. The results show that such constraints should be treated as testable geological interpretations rather than fixed representations of the subsurface. Overall, this thesis provides a connected framework for understanding, recovering, and evaluating geological information from UAV-borne magnetic and radiometric data.

title: AI explained: a guide for non-technical readers
abstract: AI Explained: A Guide for Non-Technical Readers builds understanding of artificial intelligence from first principles rather than diving in at the top. Written by experienced policy and technical experts, the book walks through rules and logic-based approaches, statistical methods, neural networks, machine learning, and generative models in accessible, structured terms. Each major section concludes with a dedicated use-cases chapter grounding abstract concepts in practical scenarios drawn from healthcare, law, and business. Rather than teaching readers how to build or deploy AI, the book answers a more fundamental question: how do these systems achieve the outcomes they produce? Coverage of AI policy, ethics, and societal impact rounds out the treatment, informed directly by the authors' advisory roles with governments and international bodies.

title: Dodging impossibilities in quantum cryptography : on the feasibility of one-time programs, signing quantum states, and cryptography without one-way functions
abstract: Cette thèse par articles étudie les frontières de la faisabilité cryptographique quantique, en démontrant comment les propriétés singulières de l’information quantique peuvent être exploitées pour contourner des résultats d’impossibilité fondamentaux. Nous explorons trois régimes distincts dans lesquels des théorèmes d’impossibilité (≪ No-Go ≫) traditionnels sont surmontés : la réalisation de programmes à usage unique dans un modèle où la mémoire quantique de l’adversaire est de taille bornée, la signature de messages quantiques au moyen de contraintes temporelles et la réalisation de primitives cryptographiques sans avoir à supposer l’existence de fonctions à sens unique. La première partie de ce travail exploite le modèle de mémoire quantique bornée (Bounded Quantum Storage Model ), dans lequel les adversaires sont limités quant à leur mémoire quantique. Nous démontrons que cette limitation physique permet la construction de programmes à usage unique — une forme puissante d’obfuscation de programmes dont l’impossibilité est prouvée dans le modèle standard. De manière cruciale, puisque la sécurité découle de contraintes de mémoire plutôt que de difficulté calculatoire, nos constructions atteignent une sécurité au sens de la théorie de l’information. Nous utilisons les programmes à usage unique pour développer, pour la première fois, des applications cryptographiques fondamentales, notamment le chiffrement à clé asymétrique et les signatures numériques assortis de garanties au sens de la théorie de l’information. La deuxième contribution remet en question le paradigme établi de longue date selon lequel la signature de messages quantiques est intrinsèquement impossible. Nous introduisons les signatures dépendantes du temps, dont la sécurité est assurée par la synchronisation temporelle des processus de signature et de vérification. Nous montrons que ce cadre permet la signature d’états quantiques à l’aide de n’importe quelle fonction à sens unique et puzzle à verrou temporel (time-lock puzzle). De plus, nous démontrons qu’en recourant à des clés de vérification dynamiques qui évoluent au cours du temps, l’exigence de puzzles à verrou temporel peut être éliminée. Nous appliquons le schéma de signature à la construction du chiffrement à clé publique quantique authentifié dépendant du temps et de la monnaie quantique à clé publique. La dernière partie de la thèse contribue au corpus croissant de recherches réévaluant la nécessité fondamentale des fonctions à sens unique (OWF) en tant qu’hypothèse inimale pour une cryptographie non triviale. Plus précisément, nous fournissons une séparation en boîte noire démontrant qu’un générateur pseudo-aléatoire (PRG) augmenté d’une procédure d’échantillonnage d’entrée quantique représente une hypothèse potentiellement plus faible qu’un PRG traditionnel à échantillonnage uniforme, lequel est équivalent aux OWF. À partir de cette observation, nous montrons que des applications importantes, telles que l’authentification de messages et les mises en gage (commitments) avec communication classique, sont également séparées en boîte noire des PRG traditionnels. Cela apporte des éléments en faveur d’une nouvelle hypothèse, potentiellement plus faible, pour ces applications cryptographiques. Prises ensemble, ces contributions offrent une perspective différente des paysages dans lequel le cryptographie quantique peut-être développée. En remplaçant les hypothèses fondamentales — de la difficulté calculatoire vers des bornes de mémoire, de l’indépendance temporelle vers la dépendance temporelle, et de l’échantillonnage uniforme vers l’échantillonnage quantique — cette thèse établit qu’une gamme plus large de primitives sûres est faisable dans des modèles réalistes que ce qui est possible dans le modèle calculatoire standard.

Nous utilisons les programmes à usage unique pour développer, pour la première fois, des applications cryptographiques fondamentales, notamment le chiffrement à clé asymétrique et les signatures numériques assortis de garanties au sens de la théorie de l’information. La deuxième contribution remet en question le paradigme établi de longue date selon lequel la signature de messages quantiques est intrinsèquement impossible. Nous introduisons les signatures dépendantes du temps, dont la sécurité est assurée par la synchronisation temporelle des processus de signature et de vérification. Nous montrons que ce cadre permet la signature d’états quantiques à l’aide de n’importe quelle fonction à sens unique et puzzle à verrou temporel (time-lock puzzle). De plus, nous démontrons qu’en recourant à des clés de vérification dynamiques qui évoluent au cours du temps, l’exigence de puzzles à verrou temporel peut être éliminée. Nous appliquons le schéma de signature à la construction du chiffrement à clé publique quantique authentifié dépendant du temps et de la monnaie quantique à clé publique. La dernière partie de la thèse contribue au corpus croissant de recherches réévaluant la nécessité fondamentale des fonctions à sens unique (OWF) en tant qu’hypothèse inimale pour une cryptographie non triviale. Plus précisément, nous fournissons une séparation en boîte noire démontrant qu’un générateur pseudo-aléatoire (PRG) augmenté d’une procédure d’échantillonnage d’entrée quantique représente une hypothèse potentiellement plus faible qu’un PRG traditionnel à échantillonnage uniforme, lequel est équivalent aux OWF. À partir de cette observation, nous montrons que des applications importantes, telles que l’authentification de messages et les mises en gage (commitments) avec communication classique, sont également séparées en boîte noire des PRG traditionnels. Cela apporte des éléments en faveur d’une nouvelle hypothèse, potentiellement plus faible, pour ces applications cryptographiques. Prises ensemble, ces contributions offrent une perspective différente des paysages dans lequel le cryptographie quantique peut-être développée. En remplaçant les hypothèses fondamentales — de la difficulté calculatoire vers des bornes de mémoire, de l’indépendance temporelle vers la dépendance temporelle, et de l’échantillonnage uniforme vers l’échantillonnage quantique — cette thèse établit qu’une gamme plus large de primitives sûres est faisable dans des modèles réalistes que ce qui est possible dans le modèle calculatoire standard.

title: The Cardinality Ceiling: Why Agentic LLM Output Succeeds on Low-Constraint Requests and Degrades as Constraint Cardinality Rises
abstract: This paper describes a process as it is. It makes one descriptive claim: agentic large language model (LLM) output is well-suited to requests that carry few simultaneously-binding constraints, and it degrades in a predictable, enumerable way as the number of such constraints rises. The paper does not argue that practitioners should change their behavior or that products should change their design. It provides a mechanical account of why the degradation occurs, an account of why the degradation is difficult to observe in current practice, and an ordered list of the specific failure modes that appear as constraint cardinality increases. The account is grounded in first-person practitioner experience, including a documented multi-week loss and its later one-day resolution under changed constraints, and in a live design session that produced several of the enumerated failures in real time.

title: Adaptive Probabilistic Logic Programming
abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Probabilistic Logic Programming (APLP), a novel approach to intelligent systems design. The core challenge in many real-world applications is dealing with uncertainty and evolving environments. Traditional logic programming suffers from rigidity, requiring explicit definition of all rules upfront, which is often impractical and brittle. APLP addresses this limitation by dynamically adapting probabilistic logic rules based on observed execution outcomes. This is achieved through the integration of Bayesian Networks for representing uncertainty and probabilistic logic inference engines. The system iteratively updates its rules using a Monte Carlo method for decision making. The key innovation lies in the ability of the system to learn and optimize its rules in response to changing data, leading to enhanced robustness and adaptability. This paper outlines the architecture, the key components, and the core mechanism of APLP, demonstrating its potential for applications requiring intelligent decision-making in dynamic and uncertain scenarios. The system's adaptability is central to its performance, allowing it to respond effectively to unforeseen circumstances.

title: Canefield Rat: A Novel Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by Foraging Behavior
abstract: This paper introduces a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed "Canefield Rat," inspired by the foraging behavior of *Canefield rats* (genus *Neotoma*). These rats are known for their efficient and adaptive strategies in locating and exploiting food sources in complex environments. The algorithm leverages key aspects of their foraging process, including path exploration, memory of successful locations, and probabilistic decision-making, to construct a robust optimization approach. Canefield Rat utilizes a population-based search strategy combined with a memory mechanism to guide the exploration and exploitation phases. The algorithm's core components involve a fitness function, a neighborhood structure, and a probabilistic acceptance criterion. We demonstrate the efficacy of Canefield Rat through a series of test problems, comparing its performance against established metaheuristic algorithms such as Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Ant Colony Optimization (ACO). The results indicate that Canefield Rat exhibits competitive performance and offers a promising alternative for tackling various optimization challenges.

title: Title: Adaptive Resonance Network for Pattern Recognition (ARNP)
abstract: This paper presents the Adaptive Resonance Network (ARNP), a novel neural network architecture specifically designed for pattern recognition. The core innovation of ARNP lies in its dynamic weighting system, which allows the network to adapt its pattern recognition parameters based on the characteristics of the input data. This adaptive approach enhances robustness and accuracy compared to static pattern recognition methods. The paper details the architecture, training methodology, and experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of ARNP in various pattern recognition tasks. We explore the impact of the dynamic weighting system on the network's performance, highlighting its ability to generalize to unseen data.

title: Non-Linear Topological Geometry: Modeling Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper explores the potential of non-linear topological geometry to model quantum entanglement, focusing on its application to quantum information storage and processing. We propose a novel framework incorporating the concept of "quantum topological entanglement" – a dynamic and non-linear topological structure that interacts with quantum entanglement, offering a pathway toward enhanced quantum algorithms. The core mechanism involves constructing a model that dynamically evolves, leveraging the inherent properties of topological geometry to store and manipulate quantum information. We demonstrate the potential of this model through theoretical analysis and illustrative examples, suggesting significant advantages in quantum computation, particularly regarding information fidelity and entanglement generation.

title: 基于自适应的复杂系统模型生成的优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on adaptive systems models, designed to address the limitations of traditional optimization techniques in complex systems. The algorithm dynamically adjusts optimization strategies based on the system's complexity and initial state, providing a more flexible and powerful approach to model optimization. We propose a framework that leverages a hierarchical system model to represent the system, enabling the algorithm to progressively refine its optimization strategy. The paper details the design of the adaptive component, its implementation, and the results achieved through extensive simulations. We demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods in a variety of complex system optimization scenarios, showcasing its ability to effectively navigate intricate parameter spaces and achieve optimal solutions.

title: 自适应几何的量子态的计算
abstract: This paper explores the potential of utilizing dynamic adaptive mechanisms to enhance the calculation of quantum states. Traditional quantum state estimation methods often rely on static models, limiting their ability to accurately represent complex quantum systems. We propose a novel approach that dynamically adjusts the parameters of a quantum state representation, leveraging the inherent self-adaptation properties of quantum systems. This method aims to improve prediction accuracy by capturing the subtle nuances of quantum behavior, offering a significant advancement in computational capabilities. The core claim is that this dynamic adaptive system will yield superior results compared to static approaches, particularly for intricate quantum systems.

title: Hyper-Dimensional Computing with Temporal Correlation
abstract: Hyper-dimensional computing (HDC) presents a compelling alternative to traditional computing paradigms, leveraging high-dimensional random vectors for efficient data representation and computation. However, a significant limitation of standard HDC lies in its inherent disregard for temporal dependencies within data, particularly crucial in applications such as time series analysis and dynamic systems modeling. This work proposes an extension to HDC that explicitly incorporates temporal correlation modeling. We achieve this by integrating recurrent neural networks (RNNs) within the HDC architecture, enabling the capture and exploitation of temporal dependencies. The resulting system demonstrates improved performance across various tasks, showcasing the potential of combining the strengths of HDC with the temporal reasoning capabilities of RNNs. We analyze the impact of different RNN architectures and parameter settings on the performance, highlighting key considerations for successful implementation. Our research contributes to a more robust and versatile HDC framework, addressing a critical gap in the current understanding and application of this technology.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum Information Encoding via Self-Adapting Geometry
abstract: This paper explores the potential of adaptive geometry, specifically within the context of hyperspace geometry, to revolutionize quantum information encoding. Traditional quantum information codes rely heavily on static parameters, limiting their adaptability and security. We propose a novel encoding scheme predicated on the dynamic properties of hyperspace geometry, enabling precise control and secure transmission of quantum information. The core mechanism involves the self-adaptive nature of hyperspace geometry, allowing for continuous adjustments to the encoded state, thereby enhancing fidelity and resilience. This research aims to demonstrate the practical benefits of this adaptive approach, offering a pathway towards more robust and versatile quantum communication systems.

abstract: This record provides the replication package accompanying the manuscript “IKC: Auditing LLM-Assisted Linux Kernel Configuration with Workload Evidence.” The package contains the source code, workload-evidence processing scripts, LLM-assisted configuration workflow, generated and realized kernel configurations, benchmark scripts, raw per-run measurements, boot-time .config files, kernel identity records, environment snapshots, security-policy records, prompts, and analysis code used in the study. title: Boongary: A Novel Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by the Boorong Fruit Bat
abstract: This paper proposes Boongary, a new metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of the Boorong fruit bat. The algorithm incorporates elements of the bat's echolocation, flight patterns, and social interactions into a novel search procedure. Boongary utilizes a dynamic parameter representation of the bat's flight, including position, velocity, and frequency, to explore the search space. The algorithm employs a combination of radial basis functions (RBF) for representing the bat's state and a modified convergence criterion based on the bat's responsiveness to obstacles. The performance of Boongary is evaluated on a suite of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in finding near-optimal solutions within reasonable computation times. The algorithm's key features include adaptability to different problem landscapes, robustness to parameter tuning, and a relatively simple implementation. The results show that Boongary offers a competitive alternative to existing metaheuristic methods, particularly in problems with complex, non-convex landscapes.

title: Integration of an ontological model of CDIO competencies into the design of educational programs: transforming educational projects into knowledge content
abstract: The Conceive–Design–Implement–Operate (CDIO) Syllabus expresses graduate competencies in natural language developed through project-based learning, yet the link between declared competencies and delivered content is maintained manually. This study proposes the CDIO Competency–Knowledge Ontology (CDIO–CKO): a decidable OWL 2 Description Logic (DL) formalization of the Syllabus connected to programs, projects, courses, learning outcomes, and knowledge-content units, paired with a parameterized transformation that converts educational projects into competency-linked units via decomposition, extraction, semantic annotation, and aggregation. Applied to one 240-ECTS mechatronics and robotics program (42 courses, 18 projects, 156 competencies), the methodology produced 1,287 individuals and 9,540 triples classifying in 2.8 s. On a 240-unit held-out test set against a three-expert gold standard, automated mapping reached precision 0.91, recall 0.86, and F1 0.88 (95% CI 0.84–0.91; system–standard κ = 0.79, expert pre-adjudication κ = 0.74). Traceable coverage rose from 0.59 to 0.84, and 23 prerequisite inconsistencies missed by routine manual review were surfaced (23 of 26 issues in a dedicated expert audit: precision 1.00, recall 0.88). Against five comparator families, the method achieved the highest F1 among the five evaluated baselines while uniquely supporting consistency checking, proficiency propagation, and an auditable evidence trail. Results are a single-program proof-of-concept; broader validation remains future work.

title: Orchestration of Methods of Scientific Data Analysis in the Review Processes
abstract: Abstract— This paper explores the problem of combining methods in the semantic analysis of scientific data and publications during review. At different stages of data processing in the SciLibRu system, various methods are used, a multilevel ontology is constructed, and a knowledge graph is populated, resulting in the formation of a new data structure distinct from the original. Each method individually serves its purpose in such a system, while their combined use leads to the emergence of new properties, which became the subject of this research. An example of an automatic peer review agent with explainable results is provided.

title: Stability of Tripartite Entangled State in Spin Trimer Coupled to a Magnetic Ion
abstract: Abstract A model of a spin-1/2 trimer coupled to a magnetic ion with spins ranging from 1/2 to 5/2 is introduced. We numerically calculate tripartite negativity of spin trimer. Numerical results show that the tripartite negativity has a nonzero plateau regardless of spin of the magnetic ion. We focus on tripartite entangled state corresponding to this plateau. As spin and exchange coupling of the magnetic ion increase, the tripartite entangled state becomes increasingly stable with respect to changes in external magnetic field and temperature. This phenomenon originates from the fact that internal magnetic field formed by the magnetic ion compensates the external magnetic field applied to spin trimer.

title: A comprehensive catalog of hydroacoustic sources using the International Monitoring System network
abstract: As part of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, six hydrophone stations of the International Monitoring System transmit continuous data in real time. These stations have recorded low-frequency underwater acoustic waves propagating in the SOund Fixing And Ranging channel for decades. Automated processing of this large data volume is desirable, particularly to discriminate records by source type. However, no catalog currently exists. We present a methodology based on a rule-based expert system to establish such a catalog, covering seven source types: earthquakes, volcanic activity, cryospheric activity, whales, vessels, airguns, and chemical explosions. The catalog consists of 49 452 events from moored hydrophone stations, with an assignment error of less than 1%. Because the process is interpretable and reproducible, the catalog can be readily expanded to incorporate additional inputs. This catalog can be used to identify and analyze specific source types in greater detail.

title: Framework Summary
abstract: This chapter categorizes AI capabilities into perception, analytical, generative, and agentic AI, and formal data levels into raw, structured, context, and action data. It introduces the CRAFT assessment framework, which evaluates data completeness, retrievability, accuracy, freshness, and traceability, and distinguishes data usage for inference and training. The chapter details data thresholds for AI use cases, diagnostic signals, and responses for CRAFT, and four failure modes in AI production, emphasizing leadership misunderstanding as a root cause. It highlights that failure modes can overlap, such as traceability and accuracy issues co-occurring, and that action data completeness depends on context data coverage. Additionally, it presents a 26-characteristic inference matrix across five CRAFT dimensions and four data levels, discusses agentic AI dependencies, and outlines CRAFT checks for data levels and infrastructure portability, concluding with use case-specific thresholds and implementation patterns for data levels.

title: Privacy Amplification Without Independence: How Far Negative Dependence Carries the Guarantees of Poisson Subsampling
abstract: Poisson subsampling is the default sampler in differentially private optimization because its independence makes privacy amplification tractable. Practical systems, however, are moving toward structured participation: random allocation (balls-in-bins), per-epoch allocation, random check-ins, schemes widely believed to be at least as private as Poisson subsampling at the matched rate. We isolate the probabilistic mechanism behind this belief and delimit it exactly, for Gaussian mechanisms up to correlated-noise matrix mechanisms. (1) If the participation indicator vector is negatively associated (NA), then at every integer Rényi order $α\ge2$, exactly at all finite parameters, its remove-direction Rényi divergence is dominated by that of the marginal-matched independent scheme. For fixed gradient sequences, this extends to the mechanism level whenever the noise strategy's Gram matrix is sign-balanced, an $O(t^2)$-checkable condition. (2) The integer-order restriction is essential. For random allocation with $k=1$, we prove a linear law for the Rényi-difference criterion: at large $t$, dominance reverses for every $α<3/2$, including KL divergence, while the crossing order tends to $3/2$ independently of $σ$. (3) We also localize the known failure of rate-matched Poisson domination exactly: below $(1-q)^t$, the hockey-stick ordering reverses, so substituting the Poisson pair into composition machinery is unsound. An upper-tail argument yields a finite crossover $γ_\star$, connecting this threshold picture to the Rényi boundary at $3/2$. Together, these results give a substitution map for privacy accounting: when Poisson-based computations remain sound for structured participation, where they fail, and what sound alternatives cost in deployment.

title: A Benchmark for Vehicle Attribute Classification in Cross-Domain Surveillance Scenarios
abstract: Vehicle attribute analysis is a key component of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), supporting applications such as vehicle identification, traffic monitoring, and forensic investigation. However, models trained under controlled conditions often degrade in real surveillance scenarios due to changes in viewpoint, occlusion, illumination, and sensor characteristics. This paper introduces Unconstrained Vehicle Identification Benchmark (UVIB), a benchmark for evaluating three operational vehicle-analysis tasks: front/rear orientation, occlusion-related suitability for Vehicle Make and Model Recognition (VMMR), and color clarity. The benchmark contains 84,835 vehicle images from seven public Brazilian datasets, grouped into surveillance and general acquisition domains, with unified binary annotations that were not jointly available in the original sources. Four representative architectures, EfficientNetV2-S, ResNet-50, ViT/B-16, and YOLO11s-cls, are evaluated under mixed-domain, cross-domain, and cross-dataset protocols. The results show that domain shift has a stronger impact than architecture choice, with substantial degradation in cross-domain settings, especially for VMMR suitability and color clarity. While orientation generalizes more reliably, VMMR suitability remains affected by class imbalance and ambiguous occlusions, and color clarity is highly sensitive to illumination and sensor modality. These findings highlight the need for benchmarks and evaluation protocols that explicitly measure operational robustness beyond standard in-domain accuracy. The proposed benchmark is publicly available at https://github.com/UFPR-IPASP-PR/uvib-vehicle-attributes/.

title: Matched Queries for Curvature and Density at Branching Junctions
abstract: At a junction, a score field can reveal weighted tangent rays, yet these first-order quantities do not determine how individual branches bend or how their densities change away from the center. Recovering this missing information is necessary for describing local continuation beyond a single point, but finite observations must separate branchwise second-order effects while allowing error in the estimated center. We address this inverse problem using matched score queries at noise scales $σ$ and $λσ$. For a finite union of $C^{2,α}$ half-branches in $\mathbb{R}^D$, the normalized score has the expansion $F_σ=F_0+σG+O(σ^{1+α})$. Matched subtraction cancels the tangent contribution and exposes $G$, which depends linearly on branchwise curvature and log-density slope. Given tangent directions and weights on distinct rays, $G$ uniquely identifies all $sD$ branch parameters, and $sD$ scalar component observations are necessary. An $O(σ^2)$ center error introduces $D$ translation modes, leading to $(s+1)D$ observations under full-rank calibration, except for a translation-invariant full line. We also establish a perturbation bound and a conditional kernel-density-estimation rate. Experiments reproduce the predicted population and $N^{-1/5}$ trends and remain full rank up to $D=20$ with 16 supplied branches. In end-to-end tests for $D=3$--$5$, a known-count first-order frontend yields full rank in all 135 population systems and a median relative jet error of 0.132. With strong first-order error, matched responses reduce median parameter error by a factor of 49.4 relative to naive tangent subtraction.

title: RingMoClaw: An Experience-Inspired Multi-Agent Framework for Self-Evolving Research in Remote Sensing
abstract: Remote sensing visual models have continuously advanced various interpretation tasks. However, the research process behind model improvement still heavily relies on manual expertise, requiring extensive trial-and-error iterations in model design, data processing, and performance diagnosis. Existing agent-based approaches mainly focus on task execution and workflow orchestration, while lacking the capability of autonomous research iteration for continuous performance optimization. To address this issue, we propose RingMoClaw, an experience-inspired self-evolving multi-agent framework for remote sensing visual interpretation. RingMoClaw integrates a research branch, a quality-control branch, and a dual-stream dynamic experience bus to establish a closed-loop optimization process covering strategy generation, experiment execution, independent review, and experience accumulation. The heterogeneous Critic mechanism provides stage-wise diagnosis and feedback, while the dual-stream experience bus incorporates external knowledge and internal experimental experience to guide strategy evolution and eliminate ineffective searches. Extensive experiments on four remote sensing downstream tasks, including object detection, scene classification, semantic segmentation, and change detection, demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of RingMoClaw. Compared with the corresponding baseline models, RingMoClaw improves performance by 1.84\% mAP$_{50}$ on object detection and achieves consistent gains across the other three tasks, while reducing the required evolution steps by over 40\% compared with existing research automation frameworks. These results suggest that RingMoClaw offers a feasible route from task execution toward continuous research driven model evolution in remote sensing.

title: BrainDiff: Longitudinal Report Generation for Multimodal Brain MRI
abstract: Neuroradiologists rarely read a brain MRI in isolation, yet automated brain-MRI report generation has been built almost entirely for single studies. Temporal analysis has been explored on chest radiography and chest CT, but to our knowledge, longitudinal reporting for brain MRI, where interval change is often subtle and spatially distributed, remains unaddressed. We present BrainDiff, the first longitudinal vision-language system for brain MRI. BrainDiff outperforms both frontier general-purpose and single-study neuroimaging models on the same patient pairs. Moreover, BrainDiff retains 91% of internal RadGraph-XL entity+relation F1 (rg_er) on an external, cross-hospital cohort. Beyond the system, we contribute three analyses. First, we identify two independent grounding levers: a counterfactual objective with prior-report dropout, which increases measured image reliance by ~47%, and a staged curriculum. Together, these interventions raise image reliance 2.5-fold from the baseline. Second, we provide a factorial over prior-report availability and image identity, isolating a visual contribution of +0.0387 rg_er, which grows when the prior report is withheld. Third, a cheap change-decodability test for candidate backbones shows that interval change is decodable far more weakly than single-study pathology (0.60 vs. 0.77 AUROC). Code is publicly available at https://github.com/jhuldr/BrainDiff.

title: AI-Driven Privacy, Security, And Trusted Commercialization Frameworks for Digital Commerce and Microservice Architectures
abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into digital commerce, social e-commerce, small and medium-sized business (SMB) platforms, and microservice-based information systems has created a complex intersection of privacy, cybersecurity, commercialization, and operational governance requirements. Conventional approaches frequently address these dimensions independently, creating architectural and governance gaps when AI systems operate across distributed data environments and heterogeneous service infrastructures. This research develops a conceptual integrated framework that connects federated privacy-preserving analytics, zero-knowledge verification, trusted AI commercialization, incentive-aware recommendation infrastructure, and risk-based application security. The methodology synthesizes the provided literature to construct an architectural model consisting of privacy, intelligence, trust, security, and commercialization layers. Particular attention is given to the integration of federated learning with differential privacy and zero-knowledge verification in digital advertising, alongside multi-tenant AI infrastructure and hybrid SAST–DAST–SCA–IAST security assessment for microservice environments. The analysis indicates that privacy-preserving AI and security automation should be treated as mutually reinforcing components rather than isolated controls. The proposed framework also identifies trade-offs involving privacy utility, computational complexity, interoperability, tenant isolation, and governance. The study contributes a research-oriented architecture for organizations seeking to deploy commercially viable AI systems while maintaining privacy and security assurance across distributed digital ecosystems.

title: Methodological study on topic modeling based on hospital needlestick injury reports: comparison of LDA and BERTopic in risk identification and management decision support
abstract: ObjectiveTaking the hospital needlestick injury report as the application scenario,to construct a comprehensive assessment framework of "theme quality⁃interpretability⁃action transformation⁃technical characteristics" to compare the potential Dirichlet scores,the differences between the two topic modeling methods,LDA and the Deep Learning Topic Framework Based on Pre⁃trained Language Models(BERTopic),in risk identification and management decision support,and input the theme⁃driven intervention suggestions.MethodsA total of 160 needlestick injury reports were collected from a tertiary hospital between January 2018 and September 2025.After preprocessing including Chinese word segmentation,stop⁃word removal,and synonym merging,LDA and BERTopic models were trained separately.Model comparison was conducted using topic coherence,expert blind evaluation,and technical indicators such as training time,parameter sensitivity,and degree of automation.The resulting topics were then mapped onto a tiered intervention framework to formulate actionable countermeasures.ResultsBoth models identified key risk scenarios including blood specimen collection, needle withdrawal/needle handling,and complex procedures in special departments.LDA generated five macro⁃level topics,suitable for rapid overview and routine monitoring.BERTopic generated four semantically coherent topics and one noise cluster, which more clearly delineated actionable scenarios such as blood collection chain risks among intern nurses,systemic failure in post-needle processing,and exposure in high⁃infection⁃risk cases.The topic coherence scores for BERTopic and LDA were 0.587 and 0.452, respectively.The overall expert rating scores were 4.555 and 3.944,respectively.Training times were 182 seconds and 45 seconds,respectively.ConclusionBERTopic demonstrates superior advantages in semantic depth and action translatability, making it suitable for root cause analysis and targeted improvement initiatives.LDA is better suited for rapid daily screening and trend monitoring.This study recommends a tiered application strategy of "routine LDA monitoring plus periodic BERTopic deep dives" in hospitals.The topic results can be transformed into structured interventions and evaluation indicators targeting populations,workflows,and devices,thereby forming a closed⁃loop management cycle of risk identification⁃intervention⁃review.

title: A Differential Privacy-Based Learning Path Optimization Algorithm for Distributed-Network Industry Operation and Maintenance Skills
abstract: In distributed network operation and maintenance (O&M) systems, skill-training behavior data are scattered across enterprise sites, training platforms, edge servers, and field terminals, so centralized learning-path optimization risks exposing sensitive information such as engineers’ response feedback, weak skill points, and training stages. This study develops DP-DLPO, a differential privacy-based distributed learning path optimization algorithm with five modules: local training-state encoding, learning path graph modeling, differential privacy perturbation, adaptive privacy budget allocation, and quality-aware federated aggregation. Each edge node uploads only model updates after gradient pruning and noise perturbation, and the cloud server aggregates updates by sample size, update quality, and noise intensity to generate a global path optimization strategy. Simulation results show DP-DLPO achieves an F1-score of 0.854, NDCG@10 of 0.817, and path completion rate of 0.843, outperforming DP-FedAvg and FedRec-DP. With privacy budget ε = 2, the model maintains strong performance while keeping attack success at 0.094, and as nodes increase from 10 to 200, F1 decreases only from 0.858 to 0.833 - showing good scalability and path interpretability for privacy-preserving skill-path optimization in industrial network O&M systems.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum State Modeling
abstract: This paper presents an adaptive quantum state modeling approach leveraging quantum entanglement and non-locality to enhance the accuracy of quantum system simulations. Traditional modeling methods often rely on classical algorithms, but this approach utilizes quantum entanglement and non-locality to offer a novel computational perspective. The core mechanism involves constructing an implicit model utilizing quantum entanglement and non-locality, leading to more precise simulation of quantum system behavior. This work aims to address limitations of existing methods and explore potential advancements in quantum computing through this innovative approach.

title: ## Capixaba Nectar-feeding Bat Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed the "Capixaba Nectar-feeding Bat" algorithm (CNBA), inspired by the foraging behavior of the Capixaba nectar-feeding bat (*Vampyrum minus*), a species known for its efficient and adaptable searching strategy. The algorithm mimics the bats' unique approach to locating nectar sources, incorporating elements such as echolocation, flight path optimization, and social interaction. The core of the CNBA lies in a modified version of the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) framework, where each particle represents a potential solution. The algorithm utilizes a bat-inspired communication mechanism to dynamically adjust particle velocities and positions, leveraging a concept of "echo loudness" and "social influence" analogous to the bats' echolocation and social dynamics. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through theoretical analysis and simulation studies, showcasing its potential in solving complex optimization problems. Specifically, we evaluate the CNBA on the Rastrigin and Sphere test functions, demonstrating its competitive performance compared to established metaheuristic algorithms like PSO and Genetic Algorithm (GA). The algorithm's design aims for improved convergence speed and robustness, particularly in challenging landscapes with multiple local optima. The paper concludes by discussing future research directions and potential applications of the CNBA.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning with Dynamic Knowledge Graphs
abstract: This paper introduces a novel neuro-symbolic reasoning system leveraging dynamic knowledge graphs. The core idea is to seamlessly integrate the perceptual capabilities of neural networks with the logical inference power of symbolic reasoning. The system dynamically evolves a knowledge graph, guided by the features extracted by a neural network. This creates a symbiotic relationship where the neural network learns from the knowledge graph, and the knowledge graph is continuously refined by the neural network's output. We explore the potential of this approach for building more robust and explainable AI systems, particularly in scenarios requiring adaptive reasoning. The system's architecture comprises a neural network for feature extraction and a dynamic knowledge graph, constantly updated through a defined inference process. We outline the key components and their interactions, emphasizing the dynamic nature of the knowledge graph and its crucial role in enabling adaptive reasoning. The system's effectiveness is demonstrated through a theoretical framework and proposed mechanisms for continuous learning and refinement.

title: Quantum State's Adaptive Geometry Deformation
abstract: Quantum state modeling has long been a significant challenge in the field of quantum computation and information processing. Traditional approaches often rely on static state representations, limiting the ability to accurately predict system behavior and identify subtle geometric structures that influence performance. This paper introduces a novel method based on the adaptive geometry of quantum states, aiming to revolutionize this process through a more dynamic and insightful approach. We propose a framework that dynamically adjusts the quantum state's geometry during computation, enabling a more precise and comprehensive modeling of quantum systems. This method is designed to uncover hidden geometric relationships between the system's structure and its computational capabilities, ultimately leading to improved quantum algorithms and a deeper understanding of fundamental quantum mechanics. The core mechanism involves constructing a geometric transformation model, employing iterative calculations to identify the most critical geometric features driving the system's behavior. This results in a new way of analyzing quantum states that goes beyond static representations.

title: Algorithmic Emergent Information Extraction (AEIE)
abstract: This paper introduces Algorithmic Emergent Information Extraction (AEIE), a novel machine learning framework designed to automatically extract meaningful information from complex, non-linear systems. Traditional machine learning frequently relies on manual feature engineering, limiting the potential for discovering inherent structure. AEIE leverages a dynamic resonance mapping algorithm to continuously analyze system output, generating representations of underlying patterns, thereby enabling automated discovery of complex relationships. The core claim is that AEIE can outperform traditional methods by explicitly modeling and extracting information through algorithmic emergence – a process where the system itself generates new insights. This work explores the design and implementation of the Dynamic Resonance Mapping algorithm, detailing its theoretical foundation and preliminary experimental results demonstrating its efficacy in extracting information from simulated data sets. We present a case study focusing on a synthetic dataset designed to highlight the algorithm's capabilities.

title: Brants' Whistling Rat
abstract: This paper introduces a novel metaheuristic algorithm, "Brants' Whistling Rat," inspired by the unique vocalizations of the whistling rat ( *Rattus norvegicus*). The algorithm leverages the rat's ability to mimic sounds and its exploratory behavior within complex environments to enhance the performance of other optimization techniques. Brants' Whistling Rat employs a combination of a memory-based exploration strategy mimicking the rat's auditory memory, and a local search mechanism based on probabilistic movement reflecting the rat's exploratory gait. The algorithm's core is a modified Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) framework where each particle represents a potential solution. The memory component dynamically adjusts particle velocities based on previously visited regions of the search space, prioritizing areas with promising solutions. Furthermore, a probabilistic movement component introduces randomness into particle updates, simulating the rat's unpredictable movements. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through simulations across several benchmark problems, showcasing its ability to converge to optimal or near-optimal solutions with competitive efficiency compared to established metaheuristics. The key parameters of the algorithm – memory weight, probabilistic movement strength, and PSO parameters – are discussed, and their impact on the overall performance is analyzed. The algorithm's adaptability and potential for application in diverse optimization problems are highlighted.

title: ## Bougainville Monkey-faced Bat Inspired Metaheuristic Algorithm for Complex Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper presents a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed the Bougainville Monkey-faced Bat (BMB) algorithm, inspired by the foraging behavior of the Bougainville monkey-faced bat (Micronycterus junius). These bats exhibit a unique and remarkably efficient foraging strategy characterized by a complex interplay of flight patterns, echolocation, and social interaction. The BMB algorithm leverages these observed characteristics to develop a new optimization approach suitable for tackling complex, non-linear, and multi-objective problems. The core of the algorithm involves a population of bats, each representing a potential solution. Bats dynamically adjust their flight paths based on a combination of individual experience, social influence (mimicking successful neighbors), and an exploration-exploitation balance governed by a novel "echo intensity" parameter. We detail the algorithm's design, including the key parameters influencing its performance, and provide a theoretical analysis of its convergence properties. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through a series of benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving near-optimal solutions in a reasonable timeframe. The results indicate that the BMB algorithm offers a competitive alternative to established metaheuristic methods, particularly in scenarios requiring adaptability and robust exploration.

title: Blyth's Flying Fox: A Novel Metaheuristic Optimization Algorithm Inspired by the Flight of a Unique Bird
abstract: This paper introduces Blyth's Flying Fox (BFF), a new metaheuristic optimization algorithm inspired by the remarkable flight capabilities of the Blyth's Flying Fox ( *Pteropus blythii*), a large fruit bat known for its exceptional maneuverability and precision in flight. BFF leverages the bat's echolocation and flight dynamics to develop a novel search strategy. The algorithm employs a population of 'bats' representing potential solutions, utilizing a 'pulse' emission and reception mechanism analogous to echolocation to evaluate solution quality and guide exploration and exploitation. Specifically, BFF utilizes a dynamic adjustment of pulse frequency and amplitude based on a local neighborhood search, combined with a global convergence mechanism driven by the average fitness of the population. We demonstrate the efficacy of BFF through simulations on a range of benchmark optimization problems, showcasing its competitive performance compared to established metaheuristic algorithms such as Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Genetic Algorithms (GA). The algorithm's simplicity, adaptability, and potential for further refinement make it a promising addition to the metaheuristic optimization landscape.

title: Hierarchical Graph Neural Networks for Complex System Modeling
abstract: Hierarchical Graph Neural Networks (H-GNNs) offer a promising approach to modeling complex systems by learning representations at multiple levels of granularity. This paper explores the design and evaluation of a novel H-GNN architecture that leverages a 'nested graph' approach and 'feature aggregation' to enhance the model's ability to capture intricate relationships within a system. We introduce a new mechanism for refining representations across different levels of abstraction, resulting in improved performance across a range of benchmark datasets. The proposed H-GNN demonstrates significant advancements in capturing nuanced patterns and relationships, ultimately providing a robust framework for complex system modeling.

title: Looking Things Up Before Speaking: A Historical Development Review of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of RAG and retrieval as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: From Model Explainability to Operational Transparency in Agentic AI: A Transparency-by-Design Framework for Critical Energy Systems Under the EU AI Act
abstract: Agentic AI can coordinate distributed energy resources, invoke tools, revise plans, and act through multiple interacting agents. In critical energy systems, however, model-level explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) cannot reveal how goals, constraints, tools, delegations, authority, human intervention, and system changes combine to produce an operational action. This creates a regulatory and engineering gap wherever EU AI Act requirements for transparency, record-keeping, and human oversight apply. The transparency-by-design framework addresses this gap by treating operational transparency as a compositional property created through evidence continuity across model, agent, interaction, system, and lifecycle levels. It translates five regulatory transparency functions into eight components, a seven-stage gated lifecycle, stakeholder responsibilities, evidence artefacts, and acceptance criteria. Together, these elements specify what must be transparent, to whom, when, and how adequacy should be assessed and maintained. Regulatory analysis and thematic synthesis of 101 studies provide the evidence base. Application to an agentic virtual power plant demonstrates how forecasts, goals, plan revisions, inter-agent decisions, operator interventions, execution records, and system versions can be joined within one reconstructable evidence chain. The framework extends XAI from local model explanation to lifecycle-wide operational transparency for compliance-oriented development, without claiming legal conformity or field effectiveness.

title: QUANTUM COMPUTING IN THE NISQ ERA: EVALUATING THE PARADIGM SHIFT FROM CLASSICAL ARCHITECTURES TO FTQC
abstract: The transition from classical to quantum computation marks a shift from deterministic binary logic to a probabilistic, entanglement‑driven framework able to address problems beyond classical reach. Today’s Noisy Intermediate ‑ Scale Quantum era features devices that lack full error correction yet already point toward larger, modular systems designed for fault‑tolerant operation. This paper examines the evolving paradigm shift from classical and NISQ ‑ era machines toward practical fault‑tolerant quantum computing, focusing on how advances in physical qubit technologies, control architectures, and error‑correction strategies are converging to bridge noisy prototypes and scalable, useful machines. We synthesize insights from historical semiconductor scaling trends, contemporary roadmaps from leading institutions and industry, and emerging modular designs with real‑time error decoding. Our analysis shows that while challenges around decoherence, connectivity, and classical co‑processing remain, coordinated progress in hardware, control, and software is laying a coherent foundation for future quantum platforms. The work concludes that quantum computing is maturing into a strategically significant paradigm, poised to redefine the limits of computation in simulation, optimization, and secure communication.

title: Geochemical exploration possibility for mineral deposits hidden under glaciers in the Arctic regions
abstract: Based on the results of geochemical studies conducted in the area of ​​the high-mountain gold ore deposit Kumtor (Middle Tien Shan), the author concludes that it is possible to explore for ore deposits hidden under glaciers in the Arctic. The study covers both cold and warm glaciers: Petrov, Sary-Tor, Davydov, Lysy, No. 354 and Boordu, overlapping gold-tungsten-sulfide ore bodies of the Kumtor deposit. It has been established that cryogenic geochemical fields (CGF) are formed in the ice on the surface of glaciers in the epicenter of ore bodies. The structure of the CGF on glaciers of the Kumtor deposit is characterized by qualitative (chemical elements and compounds) and quantitative (concentration of elements, extent of halos) indicators, regularly distributed in the ice on the surface of glaciers. The chemical composition of the glacier CGF reflects the composition of ore bodies and endogenous halos of the Kumtor deposit. The paper characterizes the features of the CGF formed on the surface of glaciers at the epicenters of ore bodies with an established ice thickness of up to 175 m. The extent of geochemical anomalies of the CGF on the surface of glaciers from the epicenter of the ore body in the direction of ice movement varies from 50-100 to 600 m. Recommendations are given for the use of the CGF in forecasting and exploration work in the glacial regions of the Arctic.

title: Graph Neural Networks for Medicine Recommendation Systems: Focus on Temporal, Heterogeneous, and Explainable Graph Learning
abstract: Artificial intelligence has substantially enhanced clinical decision support systems in recent years, and intelligent medicine recommendation systems are among its most important applications. The non-Euclidean, complex, and non-homogeneous relationships among patients, diseases, medications, and drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are difficult to model with traditional machine learning approaches. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been adopted to address these issues because they constitute an effective paradigm for exploiting structured relational healthcare information. This paper presents a comprehensive review of GNN-based medicine recommendation systems, covering architectural design, graph construction methods, and learning processes. Major models, including GAMENet, SafeDrug, GraphCare, MedGCN, and A-GSTCN, are examined; these approaches combine static, temporal, heterogeneous, and multimodal graphs to model the interactions among patients, drugs, and diseases. Comparisons on benchmark datasets, including MIMIC-III, NMEDW, DialMed, and ZJ-CVD, indicate that GNN-based models achieve higher precision, recall, F1 score, and AUC-ROC than traditional machine learning models, underscoring the benefit of modeling relational and temporal dependencies. Key challenges, such as data sparsity, scalability, computational complexity, interpretability, and privacy in electronic health records, are also addressed. Future research directions, including explainable GNN designs, privacy-preserving learning, federated learning, differential privacy, graph pruning, and lightweight GNN architectures, are explored to improve trustworthiness and deployment viability in clinical settings. This survey provides a structured overview of state-of-the-art GNN-based medicine recommendation frameworks and serves as a foundation for developing safe, interpretable, and scalable clinical decision systems.

title: Architecture of large language models and fuzzy logic control of text generation
abstract: The monograph is devoted to the mathematical foundations and software implementation of the architecture of large GPT class language models with fuzzy logic control of text generation. The tokenization of BPE, the mechanism of multi-headed self-awareness, the architecture of the transformer block, pre-training and fine-tuning are considered. A trilogy of fuzzy logic controllers and a FuzzyLLM closed-loop controller have been developed. A 3.1-fold decrease in the decoding entropy has been experimentally confirmed. The accuracy of the spam classifier is 95.67%. The code of 219 cells is reproduced without a GPU. It is intended for graduate students, researchers in the field of machine learning, natural language processing and fuzzy set theory.

title: Automated Text Classification with Relevance to Bloom's Taxonomy Levels: A Systematic Review
abstract: For scalable and impartial educational assessments, it is becoming increasingly crucial to automatically classify texts into Bloom&s;s Taxonomy levels. This systematic review examines recent approaches for this task, including machine learning algorithms and natural language processing techniques. The study categorizes methods based on their core principles—deep learning architectures, supervised classifiers, and feature-based models—and evaluates the datasets and performance metrics used. Several studies report high classification accuracy, with models such as Random Forest (99.2%), SVM-SMOTE (98%), and MTBERT-Attention (97.71%) outperforming traditional techniques. Deep learning and transformer-based approaches demonstrate strong potential, though challenges like limited datasets and high computational demands persist.
